answer.label: Not scripture — the wording is from a 1965 film
answer.authorDates: Anonymous proverb · the familiar wording popularised in 1965
answer.sourceLine: This one is not in the Bible — not in the Old Testament or the New, not in any book, not in any translation. Pastors and Bible teachers say so in print, plainly and without much fuss. The wording almost everyone is actually remembering belongs to Maria in The Sound of Music (1965), who quotes it as something the Reverend Mother always says. Behind that lies a genuinely old but anonymous proverb about one door closing and another opening — and it does not mention God at all.

source.excerpt: When the Lord closes a door... somewhere He opens a window.
trail: Start with the negative, because it is the whole question. Commentators writing for Christian readers state it directly: like a number of biblical-sounding sayings, this one is not actually in the Bible. Scripture does use door imagery — Paul writes of doors being opened for his work in Acts and in both Corinthian letters — but that is a metaphor for opportunity, and none of those passages says anything about a window a pastor’s account ↗.

We will not do what the internet does next and hand you a chapter and verse it is ‘really’ from. People propose several candidates; we found no reference work that identifies a specific verse as the source of this saying, so we are not naming one. The honest finding is that the saying has no biblical parent — not that it has a hidden one.

Now the positive. In the 1965 film of The Sound of Music, Maria repeats it as the Reverend Mother’s habitual saying, in the form ‘When the Lord closes a door… somewhere He opens a window,’ and the line recurs later in the picture. The screenplay is by Ernest Lehman. That is the vector: an enormously popular film, a nun saying it, and a religious register — everything needed for an audience to file it under scripture.

And behind the film is an old, ordinary proverb, which historians of quotations trace back well before any of its famous claimants — it appears in a sixteenth-century Spanish novella and in the 1620 English translation of Don Quixote. Both the short form and the longer ‘we look so long at the closed door’ version are, in the end, anonymous the proverb’s history ↗.
source.excerptNote: Maria’s line in the 1965 film, quoting the Reverend Mother. Notice how much more tentative it is than the version people carry around: somewhere He opens a window — a hope offered by one character to herself, not a guarantee issued from a pulpit. The certainty is something the saying picked up in transit.

source.rightsNote: Two different things here, with two different statuses. The proverb about one door closing and another opening is centuries old and anonymous, and nobody owns it. The specific film wording quoted above is a line from a 1965 screenplay and a 1959 stage musical, both firmly in copyright and both actively licensed — a brief quotation with attribution, as here, is ordinary practice, but it is not free text to reproduce at length or to print on goods. If you want a version you can use without thinking about it, use the plain proverb. This is not legal advice.

author.name: The Bible
author.heading: Why people think it is scripture
author.metaLine: The collected scriptures of Judaism and Christianity · commonly credited here in error
author.bio: The Bible attracts this kind of adoption because so much of English moral vocabulary genuinely came from it, and readers reasonably assume that a saying which sounds scriptural probably is. It is far from alone in being wrongly credited: ‘God helps those who help themselves’, ‘cleanliness is next to godliness’ and ‘money is the root of all evil’ are all outside it, misremembered, or both. Nothing here bears on what scripture says or on anyone’s faith; the question on this page is narrow — where a particular English sentence came from — and the answer happens to be a film.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Almost nobody claims a verse for this one. That is what makes it interesting: it is credited to scripture by atmosphere rather than by citation, and the credit survives precisely because nobody is asked to produce a reference.

items.why: It is in no book of the Old or New Testament, in any translation. Writers addressing Christian readers say so directly, and treat it as one of a family of sayings the church has absorbed from elsewhere the article ↗.

The Bible does speak of doors being opened — Paul uses the figure in Acts and in both letters to the Corinthians — and that is very likely why the saying feels canonical. But those passages are about opportunities for his work, they never mention a window, and no reference work we found identifies any of them as this saying’s source. We are naming no verse, because doing so would be inventing a citation.

items.tag: a nun says it on screen
items.why: Maria quotes it as the Reverend Mother’s saying, and it returns later in the film. A line delivered in a convent, in a picture that most of the English-speaking world has seen, is about the most efficient possible way to make a sentence sound like scripture.

‘When one door closes, another opens’ predates every famous name attached to it, appearing in a sixteenth-century Spanish novella and in the 1620 English Don Quixote. The theological framing — God as the one doing the closing and opening — is a later addition.

Alexander Graham Bell and Helen Keller are both offered as authors of the longer version about staring too long at the closed door. Quotation researchers find the adage anonymous and older than either of them.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is what you say to someone whose plan has just collapsed, and it works because it makes a loss provisional. Not this is fine, which nobody believes, but this is not the end of the sentence — and a window rather than another door is a good image, because a window is smaller, less dignified, and not the way you meant to leave.

Finding out it is not in the Bible changes nothing about whether it is true, and that is worth saying clearly. Plenty of people have found the thought consoling and go on doing so. What changes is only the paperwork: if you are quoting it as scripture — in a sermon, a eulogy, a card — it is worth knowing that the person who said it first, as far as anyone can trace, was a fictional postulant in a musical.
context.detailsSummary: Sayings people file under scripture that are not in it
detailsBody: ‘God helps those who help themselves’ — not in the Bible; popularised in English by Benjamin Franklin’s Poor Richard’s Almanack.
‘Cleanliness is next to godliness’ — not in the Bible; a proverb given wide currency by John Wesley in a sermon.
‘Money is the root of all evil’ — a real verse, misquoted: scripture says the love of money, which is a different claim.
‘This too shall pass’ — not in the Bible; a wandering proverb usually attached to a Persian or Jewish folk tale.
‘When God closes a door, He opens a window’ — not in the Bible; the familiar wording comes from a 1965 film.
context.pull: A nun says it on screen in 1965. That is enough to make a sentence sound like scripture.
